title: Checkpoint 12: Magnus vs Stockfish (skill 0)
notes: Checkpoint after game 12, from the Italian Game: Magnus plays the yardstick, Stockfish at skill 0. Nothing is studied afterwards.

moves.thought: 5.Nxe5? Nxe5 only loses a piece for a pawn and Bxf7+ is pointless, so I play the move c3 prepared: d4 strikes the centre. After 5...exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 or 6.e5, and 5...Nxe4 6.dxc5 just wins the bishop back, so my pawn centre is safe with every capture checked.

Black's 5...Be7 leaves e5 defended only by the c6 knight, so after 6.dxe5 the natural recapture 6...Nxe5 simply drops a piece to 7.Nxe5 (nothing on d7/f6/e7 covers e5), and 6...Nxe4 runs into 7.Qd5 hitting the knight and f7. I checked that e5 cannot be met by any pawn capture and that 6...d6 7.exd6 Bxd6 or 6...Ng4 7.Bf4 both leave me a clean pawn up.

Black's knight on e4 is unsupported and short of safe squares, so I play the double-purpose 7.Qd5, hitting the loose knight while adding a second attacker to f7 — exactly the trap my own earlier game punished me for as Black (8.Bd5 after ...Ne4). I checked that d5 is immune to any pawn or piece capture (no black pawn covers it, Nb4 just loses the knight to Qxe4), that 7...Nf6/Nd6 drop a piece to exf6/exd6, and that after the only defence 7...Nc5 I keep a big initiative with Bg5 or b4.

Black's knight on e4 is completely undefended — nothing on the board guards that square — and no black pawn can ever capture on e4, so I simply take the piece. If Black tries the pawn fork ...d5, I answer Qxd5 Qxd5 Bxd5, trading queens while staying a knight and a pawn up.

I'm a full knight ahead after 8.Qxe4, so my only job is to get the king safe and simplify; I checked that g1 is hit by nothing and that the tempting Bxf7+ and Qxh7+ both just lose the piece to Kxf7/Kxh7. After 9.O-O dxe5 10.Nxe5 Nxe5 11.Qxe5 I keep the extra knight with equal pawns and a safe king.

Counting material, I'm a clean knight up (Black lost Nf6 for the e4 pawn), so my priority is to kill the tension on e5 and avoid tactics rather than grab more. 10.exd6 resolves the pawn that both ...dxe5 and ...Nxe5 were hitting; after cxd6 or Bxd6 I recapture nothing loose, my queen on e4 stays safe, and I can finish with Nbd2/Bf4 while a whole piece ahead.

I first checked every capture: Bxf7+, Qxh7+, Qxc6, Qxe7 and Bxa6 all lose material since f7/h7/c6/e7/a6 are each defended, and the tempting Bf4 hitting the queen is simply met by Qxf4 along the d6-e5-f4 diagonal with no defender. So I play the quiet Qe2, stepping the queen off e4 before ...Bf5 gains a tempo, keeping everything guarded and preparing Nbd2, Rd1 and Bf4 later.

Qxe7 loses to Nxe7 since the knight guards e7, and the Bxf7+ Rxf7 Ne5 trick only nets rook+pawn for bishop+knight while handing Black two bishops. Bd3 is safe (d3 is covered by Qe2 and no pawn can hit it), gains a tempo by hitting the g6 queen and blunting the b1-h7 diagonal, and keeps Nbd2 development available.

Black's queen on g6 sits on the b1-h7 diagonal with e4 and f5 empty, so my bishop on d3 simply takes it: Bxg6 hxg6 (or fxg6) nets queen for bishop, resolving the d3 tension in my favour instead of needing Rd1 to hold the bishop. I checked the recapture chain and Black has no check or counter-threat after the trade.

My bishop on g6 is attacked by the h7 pawn, and since I already won the queen for a bishop with 13.Bxg6, I just need to retreat it safely rather than throw it away with Bxf7+ or Bxh7+. Bd3 puts it on a safe square defended by Qe2, keeps the b1-h7 diagonal, and if Black tries ...Nb4 to hit it, cxb4 simply wins a knight.

I'm up a queen for a knight, so I just need safe development and no loose pieces — Bxh7+ is a trap since Kxh7 wins my bishop for a pawn. Nbd2 brings my last undeveloped piece out, keeps everything defended, and leaves Black with no checks or captures that hit anything.

I'm up a queen and a knight, so I just need safe consolidation: Bxh7+ loses a bishop to Kxh7 and Qe8+ loses my queen to Rxe8, both traps I checked first. Nc4 is immune to pawn attack right now, hits both Bd6 and the loose a5 pawn, and if Black retreats the bishop I simply take a5 for free.

I'm up a queen and a knight, so the simplest path is to liquidate Black's active pieces rather than grab pawns — Nxa5 fails to ...Nxa5 (the c6 knight covers a5) and Bxg6/Qe8+ just lose material. Nxd6 trades my knight for Black's strong dark-squared bishop; after cxd6 or Rxd6 nothing of mine is loose and no check or capture hits me.

I'm a full queen ahead, so I just need safe consolidation: Bf4 develops my last piece, hits the undefended rook on d6 for a tempo, and f4 can't be taken by any black piece or pawn. I checked that Rxd3 is met by Qxd3, and Bxg6 would lose a bishop to fxg6/hxg6.

I'm a whole queen up, so I just want a safe, simple material grab with tempo: Bxc7 takes a free pawn (c7 is covered by nothing — the knight on c6 and bishop on c8 don't guard it, and the b8 rook can't capture diagonally) while attacking the rook on b8. I checked Black's replies: no checks exist, Rxf3 gxf3 is harmless, and if ...Nd8 or ...Rc-something harasses the bishop it simply retreats to f4 with the pawn pocketed.

I'm already up a queen for a pawn, and Black's rook on b8 is attacked by my bishop with only the knight able to recapture via c6-b8, so Bxb8 wins rook for bishop; I checked that no pawn or other piece covers b8 and that after Nxb8 Black has no counter-tactic (Rxf3 gxf3 is harmless). Simplest material-winning line rather than fancy tries like Be5, which just loses the bishop to Nxe5.

I'm a queen and bishop up, so I only need safe consolidation: Bxg6 loses a piece to fxg6/hxg6, and any knight move off f3 opens the g4-e2 diagonal so ...Bxe2 wins my queen, while ...Nd4 would fork Qe2 and Nf3. Rfe1 defends e2, so ...Bxf3 Qxf3 and ...Nd4 Nxd4 Bxe2 Rxe2 both just win more material, and it avoids loosening the pawns around my king.

I'm up a queen and a rook, so my priority is simplification with no counterplay: Be5 attacks the f6 rook and forces a favourable liquidation — 22...Nxe5 23.Nxe5 Rxe5 24.Qxe5+ (or 22...Rxe5 23.Nxe5 Nxe5 24.Qxe5+) wins rook+knight for bishop+knight. I checked the whole capture chain: e5 is attacked twice (Rf6, Nc6) and defended twice (Nf3, Qe2), and Bd6/Bf4 would simply drop the bishop to Rxd6/Rxf4.

Black's Ne5 is attacked three times (Nf3, Qe2, Re1) and undefended, and I checked every Black unit for coverage of e5 — rook on f6 guards only the f-file and 6th rank, the f7/g6 pawns don't reach it, so Qxe5 is a clean free piece. I prefer it to Nxe5, which would let Bxe2 trade my queen for two pieces after the knight stops defending g4; after Qxe5 the only tries are ...Bxf3 gxf3 or ...Rxf3 gxf3 Bxf3, both leaving me a queen, two rooks and a bishop against a lone minor piece.

I rejected Qxf6+ (the king on g7 recaptures, losing queen for rook) and Bxg6 (f7/h7/Kg7 all cover g6), per my rule about pawn recaptures on the destination square. With a crushing material lead (Q+2R+B+N vs R+B), the only black asset is the a3 passer, so bxa3 eliminates it with no tactics in reply — after Bxf3 gxf3 or Rxf3 gxf3 nothing hits me with check.

I'm massively ahead in material (Q+2R+B+N vs R+B), so I avoid Qxf6+ (Kxf6 would trade my queen for a rook needlessly) and instead play h3, which kicks the bishop off g4, creates luft against any back-rank ideas, and either wins the bishop or forces Bxf3 gxf3 leaving me completely dominant.

I'm up a queen, two rooks, bishop and knight against rook and bishop, and I noticed Black's Bh5 is already nearly trapped (g4 and f3 are its only squares, with g6 blocked by its own pawn), so I want g4 next — but first I must defend f3, since after g4 Bxg4 hxg4 Rxf3 would grab my knight. Qd5 centralizes safely (no pawn can touch d5, and Rf5 or Rd6 just loses the rook to Bxf5 or Qxd6), guards f3 along the d5-e4-f3 diagonal, hits the loose b7 pawn, and keeps the threat of g4 winning the bishop.

Qxh5 fails to gxh5 and Qxf7+ fails to Rxf7, so I looked for a pawn move instead: 27.g4 traps the bishop on h5, since its only free diagonal square is g4 itself (g6/f7 are his own pawns), so Bxg4 hxg4 or gxh5 gxh5 nets me a piece for a pawn. I checked that g4 doesn't weaken my king — Black has no checks, and Rxf3 is answered by Qxf3 because my queen on d5 still covers f3 along the d5-e4-f3 diagonal while the g4 pawn blocks ...Bxf3.

Black's Bh5 is attacked twice (Qd5 along the 5th rank and the g4 pawn) and defended only by the g6 pawn, so gxh5 simply wins a bishop for a pawn; I verified Nf3 is not actually loose because Qd5 covers f3 along the d5-e4-f3 diagonal, so 28...Rxf3 29.Qxf3 is fine, and Black has no checks afterwards.

My Nf3 is only guarded by the queen along d5-e4-f3, so any queen move (or Re4, which blocks that diagonal) drops it to Rxf3; Qd4+ and Qe5+ also fail since the rook either captures on d4 or blocks on f6. Ne5 solves everything: the knight is defended by Re1, it frees my queen, and it threatens Nxg6/Nxf7 while nothing of mine is capturable (Rxf2 Kxf2).

I'm massively up material, and Qxf7+ is a capture with check that is safe because the knight on e5 guards f7, forcing Kh8 (Kxf7 impossible); then Ng6+ Kh7 (forced, since Kg8 is covered by my queen) and Nxf4 wins the rook too. I checked Black has no checks, captures or counter-threats against my king, so this is a clean forcing line.

My knight on e5 can simply take the rook on f7, and after Kxf7 I'm left with two rooks and a bishop against a bare king with three pawns — a trivially winning simplification that removes Black's only piece and any counterplay. I checked that nothing is left loose: the f7 recapture by the king is Black's only option, and my remaining pieces are all safe.

My knight on f7 is attacked by the black king and undefended, and Nxg5 (hxg5), Nxh6 (Kxh6) and Nh8 (Kxh8) all just dump a piece for a pawn. Ne5 retreats it to a completely safe square where it stays active, keeping my overwhelming material edge (two rooks, bishop and knight versus bare pawns) intact.

I'm up two rooks, a bishop and a knight against a bare king, so I just need to avoid tricks: Black's only captures are the g5 pawn taking on f4 or h4, so I avoid f4/h4. Nd7+ is a safe check (nothing attacks d7) that drives the king and immediately picks up the b6 pawn next move while my rooks come to the e- and d-files for mate.

Black's king on f7 guards e6/e7/e8, so the tempting Re7+ and Re8 would simply be met by Kxe7/Kxe8 — the rook is undefended there, exactly the kind of blunder my notebook warns about. Instead I centralise with Re5, which is protected by the knight on d7, keeps the e-file (and thus e6/e7/e8) covered so the king stays boxed in, and attacks the g5 pawn while my a1 rook comes to the e-file next.

I'm up two rooks, a bishop and a knight against three bare pawns, so I just need to eliminate counterplay safely; Black's g4 pawn attacks my h3 pawn, and hxg4 removes it for free. I rejected Re7+ because the rook on e7 is undefended and Kxe7 would simply win it.

I'm overwhelmingly ahead (two rooks, bishop and knight versus two bare pawns), so my only job is to avoid hanging anything while building a mating net: Re8+ fails to ...Kf7 hitting the loose rook, so I prefer Bc4+, which is immune to capture and drives the king to h8/g7 where Nf6 plus Re7/Rg5 mates quickly.

I'm a rook, bishop and knight up against two bare pawns, so I just need to grab material safely — Rg5+ loses the rook to hxg5 and Nf6/Nf8 drop the knight to Kxf6/Kxf8, while Nxb6 is attacked by nothing and removes Black's only queenside pawn. After that my king and extra pieces simply escort pawns home.

I'm up two rooks, a bishop and a knight against a bare king with one pawn, so the only risk is carelessness — Rae1 brings my last piece into the game with zero counterplay, since Black has no captures and the king is already boxed in (Re5 cuts the e-file and 5th rank, h5/g4 cover g6/f5). I avoided Re6+ because ...Kg5 lets the king wander toward my g4 pawn, while after Rae1 Black must play Kf7 or Kg7 and I mate shortly with Re7/Re8.

Black has only king moves left (the h6 pawn is blocked by my h5 pawn), so I must avoid stalemate and just build a ladder mate; Re8 is safe, leaves Black the moves Kf6 and Kh7, and sets up 40.R1e7# if the king goes to h7 (g8/f8/h8 covered by the rook and Bc4, g6 by the h5 pawn). If instead 39...Kf6 I continue 40.Nd5+ driving the king into the net.

Black has only a king and the h6 pawn against two rooks, bishop and knight, so I just need a safe forcing move with no counterplay. R1e6+ is check and the rook on e6 is protected by Bc4 (so Kxe6 is impossible), it keeps the e8 rook controlling the 8th rank and the e-file, and after Kf7 or Kg7 I can ladder the king to the edge with R8e7+/Ra6-a8 ideas.

I rejected Rxh6 because the black king on g5 simply takes the undefended rook; instead Rg6+ is check and the square g6 is protected by my h5-pawn, so the king must step to f4 or h4. On 41...Kh4 I have a forced mate with 42.Re4+ Kh3 43.Rg3# (g3 covered by f2, g4 by the rook), and on 41...Kf4 I keep a completely winning attack with Rf6+/Rf8+ while the e-file rook cuts off escape.

Black's only legal move is Kh3 (g5/g4 are covered by Rg6, g3 by f2, h5 by the g4 pawn), so I must avoid stalemate — 42.Bf1 immediately would be stalemate. Instead I route the knight to f5: 42.Nd5 Kh3 43.Ne7 Kh4 44.Nf5+ Kh3 45.Bf1#, where Nf5 guards h4, f2 guards g3, Rg6 guards g4/g5 and the bishop covers g2.

Black's king on h3 is in a mating net — f2 covers g3, Kg1 covers g2/h2, Rg6 guards g4/g5 and the g4 pawn guards h5 — so his only move is Kh4, but I must avoid stalemate by always having a check ready. 43.Ne3 forces Kh4, then 44.Nf5+ (covering h4) forces Kh3, and 45.Bf1 is mate.

Black's king on h4 has only h3 available (f2 guards g3, Rg6 guards g4/g5, g4 guards h5), so Ng2+ forces Kh3, and then Bf1 is mate since the bishop covers h3/g2, Ng2 covers h4, f2 covers g3 and my king on g1 covers h2.

The move list flags Re3# — the rook on e3 covers the whole third rank while my knight on g2 guards h4 and f4, the g4 pawn and Rg6 seal the g-file, and g2 is defended by my king, so the black king has no escape.
